name: tree-sitter
summary: A parser generator and incremental parsing library that produces concrete syntax trees, reuses edited tree structure, and exposes a small embeddable C runtime.

features.name: Grammar-to-concrete-syntax-tree generation
features.description: Tree-sitter grammars generate parsers whose concrete syntax tree nodes correspond to terminal and non-terminal grammar symbols, with precedence, associativity, conflicts, fields, and hidden rules available to shape the tree.
benefits: Provides a structured representation closely connected to source syntax
Makes grammar-specific names and fields available to downstream tools
costs: Grammar design must balance readable trees against parsing conflicts
The generated tree remains language-grammar specific

features.name: Incremental tree reuse after edits
features.description: An edited syntax tree can be given to the parser together with an input edit so that a new tree is produced while internally sharing structure with the old tree.
benefits: Supports reparsing workflows such as editor updates
Can avoid rebuilding unchanged portions of a syntax tree
costs: Callers must keep byte and point ranges synchronized with edits
Individual tree instances are not thread safe and require copying for concurrent use

features.name: Embeddable parser runtime
features.description: The documented runtime is written in C11, has no runtime dependencies, and exposes parser, language, tree, and node objects through a C API that can be incorporated into another build.
benefits: Permits use from editors and other host applications
Keeps the runtime boundary small for embedding
costs: Host applications must provide language grammars and manage object lifetimes
Bindings and language composition add integration-specific concerns

mathematical_views.question: Which parts of a concrete syntax tree may be reused when a source range changes?
assumptions: A tree is modeled as nodes with source ranges and parent-child relations
An input edit correctly describes old and new byte and point ranges
The model abstracts parser heuristics, allocator behavior, and exact reuse extent

mathematical_views.question: How do grammar symbols and parser conflict-resolution rules determine the labels and shape exposed to syntax consumers?
assumptions: Grammar rules are production descriptions and visible nodes are labels in the resulting tree
Precedence, associativity, and explicit conflicts determine one or more admissible parses
This is an explanatory model and does not claim a unique tree for every ambiguous grammar

benefits: Useful syntax structure without requiring a separate semantic model
costs: Grammar choices and conflict declarations affect tree usability

benefits: Potentially reduces work for localized source changes
costs: Edit bookkeeping and concurrency rules become part of the host contract
Applications must integrate grammar generation, builds, and memory ownership
